title: The march to Delhi, 1716
hook: hundreds of Sikhs are paraded and executed daily, and tradition says none renounced their faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud walls at Gurdas Nangal, and the long faithfulness called sidak. Your line was they held on. Who did you help toward a meal? Today is a hard day on this path. Take it slowly. Day eight hundred forty-five.

A road from Punjab to the capital, and a procession on it that was meant to be seen. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, Banda Singh among them, were taken to Delhi and paraded through the streets, chained, before crowds. This was a display. The empire wanted everyone watching to understand what happened to people who rose against it. Then came the executions, a group at a time, day after day. And tradition says that every one of the captives was offered the same way out. Today: the march to Delhi.
screen: `A PROCESSION MEANT TO BE SEEN.` → `PARADED, CHAINED, THROUGH DELHI.` → `THE SAME WAY OUT, OFFERED TO EACH.`

segments.voice: The way out was simple. Give up your faith, and live. Tradition says the offer was made, and that not one of them took it. That's the carry: none renounced. Sikhs still tell one story from those days. A mother, tradition says, went to the officials and pleaded for her young son. He isn't really a Sikh, she told them. He was caught up with the others by mistake. And she was granted his release. But when the order reached him, the young man refused it. He said, in the telling, that his mother was mistaken; he was a Sikh, and he would stay with his companions. And he died with them. It's a hard story, and Sikhs don't tell it to make anyone want to die. They tell it because of what it shows about faith that's been chosen, not inherited or assumed. He could have walked out. Nobody would have blamed him. He decided who he was out loud, at the worst possible moment. There's a Sikh word for the whole of that life: sikhi. The Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath, with their hair uncut, which for a Sikh is part of keeping faith whole. The march to Delhi is part of that memory. Today doesn't ask anything heroic of a listener. But it does leave a quiet question behind it. When it costs something small, a raised eyebrow, an awkward pause, do we say who we are, or let someone else say it for us?
screen: `GIVE UP YOUR FAITH, AND LIVE.` · `A MOTHER PLEADS; HER SON REFUSES.` · `CHOSEN, NOT ASSUMED.` · `SIKHI KEPT TO THE LAST BREATH.` · then, large: `NONE RENOUNCED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one minute of silence, and then a little more. Sit upright, the way people stand when a name is read aloud. Let the breath slow. Don't think of the details of what happened in Delhi. Just hold, in silence, the people who were offered a way out and kept their faith instead. If faces come, let them be faces you'll never know. When your mind wanders, return to the silence, as if you were standing in a crowd that has gone quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
sikhi, the Sikh way of life. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, paraded through Delhi and executed day after day, of whom tradition says none renounced it. Today's word.
Your line: none renounced. Today, in one small moment where it would be easier to stay quiet about what matters to you, say it plainly and kindly. Day eight hundred forty-five.

The title carries a year from the index; the spoken script states no date. The index hook gives 'hundreds ... daily'; the spoken script deliberately says 'a group at a time, day after day' and states no number.
'Tradition says every one of the captives was offered the same way out' and 'none renounced' follow the index; confirm.
